strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and timely gap: learning general-purpose, transferable features directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives, which the authors correctly note is under-explored relative to point-cloud representation learning.

The multi-teacher pretraining design is clean and principled: a shared 3DGS encoder with lightweight per-teacher projectors (SigLIP2 for language-aligned semantics, DINOv3 for generalist features, PE-Spatial for object-aware cues) with teacher-specific contrastive losses and PHI-S feature standardization to balance teachers.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing, spanning zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (Tab. 1), open-vocabulary instance segmentation (Tab. 2), 3D VQA (Tab. 3), point-cloud probing/finetuning (Tabs. 4–6), data efficiency (Tab. 5), and ablations (Tabs. 8–9, Fig. 8). Results are consistently strong and often SOTA (e.g., 24.6/47.7 f-mIoU/f-mAcc on ScanNet200, 19.6 mAP25 instance segmentation).

The data-efficiency claims are notable and well supported: 8.32× and 39.9× fewer training scenes than point-cloud pretraining baselines while remaining competitive, plus a clear scaling trend (Fig. 6).

The render-and-distill adaptation recipe is a practical contribution: it avoids ~1TB of precomputed pseudo-labels and provides on-the-fly out-of-domain adaptation, with a resource/time comparison (Tab. 7) and an ablation on teacher feature resolution/adaptation scenes (Fig. 5).

The point-cloud variant (using only centers/colors/normals) transferring well to point-cloud benchmarks is an interesting and non-trivial finding, supported by an instance retrieval robustness experiment (Tab. 8).

Ablations are thoughtful: teacher ablation (Tab. 9), design-choice ablation (Fig. 8), and the finding that introducing PE-Spatial in the second half of training is better than from the start, are useful and actionable.
The paper is generally clearly written and well-organized, with informative figures (PCA visualizations, qualitative VQA) and honest framing of the lift-then-align lineage from SceneSplat.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the lift-then-align paradigm was established by SceneSplat, and multi-teacher distillation from 2D foundation models (e.g., DUNE, AM-RADIO) is a well-known idea. The core novelty is applying it to native 3DGS encoding, which is a meaningful but incremental extension.

Several key technical components are deferred to the supplement: the exact 3DGS-aware augmentation equations (Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold perturbations), the contrastive loss formulation, and view sampling/pairing details. This limits full assessment of the technical soundness of these contributions from the main text alone.

Some headline results are marginal: on 3D VQA (Tab. 3) Chorus improves EM only from 14.4 to 14.8 and METEOR slightly decreases (22.9→22.5), so the VQA gains are not uniformly strong and the LLM-backbone substitution claim is weaker than presented.

The point-cloud transfer analysis, while interesting, is largely observational; the two hypotheses (3DGS as strong augmentation, data efficiency) are plausible but not conclusively disentangled, and the discussion is somewhat speculative.

Training cost of multi-teacher distillation (running three large 2D teachers) is not quantified in the main text; the resource comparison (Tab. 7) focuses on adaptation/storage rather than pretraining compute, so the efficiency claims are partial.

Comparisons across methods in Tabs. 1–2 involve different training data scales and input modalities (e.g., Mosaic3D 3D+2D, ScanNet-only vs joint-dataset), which, although annotated, make it difficult to isolate the effect of the proposed method from data scaling.

Some claims (e.g., "holistic" encoder, "state-of-the-art on a broad range of tasks") are slightly overreaching given the modest VQA improvements and the fact that on some point-cloud probing benchmarks (Tab. 4, Tab. 6) Chorus is competitive rather than clearly superior.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical validation across a broad spectrum of tasks and datasets: zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (ScanNet200, Matterport3D, ScanNet++, InteriorGS), open-vocabulary instance segmentation, VQA (ScanQA/Nr3D), linear/decoder probing, and full finetuning, with consistent gains over the strong SceneSplat and Sonata baselines (e.g., +3.2% f-mIoU and +9.0% f-mAcc on ScanNet200; +5.6% f-mIoU and +5.1% f-mAcc on InteriorGS).

The multi-teacher design is well motivated and empirically justified: the teacher ablation in Tab. 9 shows that adding SigLIP2, DINOv3, and PE-Spatial yields non-redundant, complementary gains, and Fig. 8 ablates the loss, augmentation, and contrastive choices in a clean, incremental fashion.

Strong data efficiency is convincingly demonstrated: Chorus matches or exceeds point-cloud pretraining methods while using 8.32x fewer training scenes than Mosaic3D (Tab. 1) and 39.9x fewer than the point-cloud baseline, and Tab. 5 shows clear advantages in the low-data regime (1%-20% scenes and 20-200 point annotations).

The 3DGS-aware augmentations (Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold perturbations) are a genuinely sensible and somewhat novel insight, grounded in the observation that 3DGS is an optimized parameter space rather than an i.i.d. point set; applying generic point-cloud jitter is shown to be suboptimal.

The render-and-distill adaptation recipe is a practical contribution: it removes the need for costly precomputed 3D pseudo-labels (Tab. 7 quantifies ~1TB storage and preprocessing overhead avoided), supports out-of-domain adaptation with online 2D supervision, and is validated in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6.

The point-cloud-compatible variant of the encoder is an interesting and unexpected transfer result, with a plausible mechanistic investigation (Tab. 8, Fig. 6) suggesting 3DGS pretraining acts as a strong augmentation and yields noise-robust features.
The paper is generally well organized, the pipeline figure (Fig. 2) is clear, and the design choices are justified with targeted ablations rather than asserted.
weaknesses: Originality is somewhat limited: multi-teacher distillation is well-established (the paper itself cites RADIO, DUNE, AM-RADIO for 2D multi-teacher aggregation), and the 'lift-then-align' paradigm is inherited from SceneSplat. The core novelty is applying this recipe to 3DGS with a particular teacher set plus two engineering innovations (augmentations, render-and-distill), which is a meaningful but incremental step rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

The explanation for why the point-cloud variant works well is presented as hypotheses (i and ii in Sec. 4.3) rather than demonstrated mechanisms; the evidence (Tab. 8, Fig. 6) is suggestive but not conclusive, and the claims about '3DGS pretraining behaving like a strong augmentation' remain speculative.

Several gains are marginal on individual tasks (e.g., instance segmentation 18.0 vs. 17.8 mAP25 over Mosaic3D in Tab. 2; ScanQA EM 22.9 vs. 22.9 in Tab. 3), so the headline 'state-of-the-art' claims rely on aggregating many small improvements; per-task significance is not established.

Some technical details are deferred to the supplement (contrastive loss equations, augmentation equations, view-sampling details), which makes parts of Secs. 3.2-3.4 and 4.1 harder to assess as written; the paper would be stronger if the core loss formulation were self-contained in the main text.

Chorus has the slowest inference time among compared methods (0.7s per scene vs. 0.49s Sonata and 0.25s Mosaic3D, Tab. 10), and the encoder is the largest among the 3DGS-native methods (131.3M params); the efficiency trade-off relative to its accuracy gains is not deeply discussed.

The teacher selection (SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE-Spatial) is justified post hoc by the ablation, but there is no principled analysis of which teachers are necessary or sufficient in general, or whether the three selected teachers are optimal compared to other reasonable foundation models.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper reports zero-shot semantic segmentation (Table 1), open-vocabulary instance segmentation (Table 2), VQA (Table 3), linear/decoder probing and full finetuning on five benchmarks (Tables 4, 6), data-efficiency studies (Table 5), and ablations (Tables 8, 9, Fig. 8). The breadth of the evaluation is genuinely strong for a 3DGS scene-encoding paper.

Consistent, if modest, improvements: Chorus beats SceneSplat on zero-shot ScanNet200 (+3.2% f-mIoU) and InteriorGS (+5.6% f-mIoU), and improves linear-probing mIoU on ScanNet200 (36.0 vs 28.8) and ScanNet++ (48.8 vs 40.7), suggesting the multi-teacher signal does add value.

The data-efficiency story is the most compelling result: the multi-teacher pretraining achieves competitive numbers with ~8.3x fewer training scenes than Mosaic3D and the paper provides a scaling analysis (Fig. 6) plus limited-data/limited-annotation experiments (Table 5) that support the claim.

The render-and-distill adaptation recipe is a practical, self-contained contribution: it avoids storing ~1TB of precomputed teacher features (Table 7) and yields a measurable +2.7% mIoU gain from only 100 new scenes, which is useful for out-of-domain transfer.

Reasonable ablations: the teacher ablation (Table 9) and design-choice ablation (Fig. 8) are executed thoughtfully, including a non-trivial finding about staging PE-Spatial late, and the instance-retrieval robustness test (Table 8) is a nice complement to the point-cloud experiments.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: multi-teacher distillation into a single backbone is already established in 2D (DUNE, RADIO, as the authors themselves cite), and SceneSplat already distills a single 2D teacher into a 3DGS encoder. The core contribution here is essentially adding two more teachers (DINOv3, PE-Spatial) and a projector head, which is an incremental extension of an existing paradigm rather than a new method.

The headline claims are oversold relative to the evidence. The abstract promises "state-of-the-art performance on a broad range of tasks," but the margins are often small or within noise: instance-segmentation mAP50 is +0.2 over Mosaic3D (Table 2), ScanQA EM is +0.5 (Table 3), and several probing numbers move by ~1-2 points. The "holistic" framing is not backed by a correspondingly large advance.

Table 2 actually shows a substantial regression on head classes (mAP_head 18.5 vs. 21.8 for Mosaic3D) alongside the tail-class gain the text advertises. The paper reports the +7.6 tail gain but never discusses or explains the head-class drop, which is a material omission.

The point-cloud compatibility claim is not fully apples-to-apples. The 3DGS scenes used for pretraining are derived from the same RGB-D sources as the point-cloud data, so the "39.9x fewer training scenes" comparison against Sonata conflates dataset size with the (expensive) 3DGS optimization pipeline that produced those scenes. The "to our surprise" framing also undercuts the argument that this is a designed contribution.

Efficiency claims are nuanced in ways the paper does not confront. Table 10 shows Chorus has more parameters (131.3M vs. 91.7M) and slower inference (0.70s vs. 0.65s) than SceneSplat, so the efficiency argument rests entirely on training-scene count and storage, not on model or inference cost. Similarly, the render-and-distill adaptation trades storage for online teacher inference (Table 7), which is not free.

Several core components are deferred to the supplement, including the exact forms of the 3DGS-aware augmentations and the contrastive-loss equations. Given that these are presented as contributions, having only prose descriptions in the main paper hurts clarity and makes it hard to assess whether the augmentations are principled or heuristic.

No statistical significance analysis is provided for the marginal gains, and there is no failure-case or negative-results discussion, which makes it difficult to judge how reliable the reported improvements are.

Comparison scope is somewhat narrow: the paper compares mainly against SceneSplat, Mosaic3D, Sonata, and PTv3, with no head-to-head against other 3DGS-native language encoders (e.g., LangSplat, GaussianGrasper) despite citing them, and no concurrent-work comparison.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored problem: learning general-purpose, transferable features directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives rather than from point clouds or rendered views.

Proposes a well-motivated multi-teacher pretraining framework that distills complementary signals from SigLIP2 (language-aligned), DINOv3 (generalist), and PE-Spatial (object-aware) into a shared 3DGS encoder with lightweight per-teacher projectors.

Extensive empirical validation across diverse tasks and benchmarks: zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation on ScanNet200, Matterport3D, ScanNet++, and InteriorGS; open-vocabulary instance segmentation; semantic/instance probing and finetuning; VQA; and point-cloud transfer. Tables 1-6 show broad, sometimes substantial gains (e.g., ScanNet200 f-mIoU 22.4 vs. SceneSplat 18.9; InteriorGS f-mIoU 9.0 vs. 6.1).

Strong data-efficiency story: Chorus uses about 2.92K training scenes vs. Mosaic3D's 24.3K (8.32x fewer) and the point-cloud variant uses 3,503 scenes vs. Sonata's 139,769 (39.9x fewer) while remaining competitive or better on several probing/finetuning benchmarks.

Practical render-and-distill adaptation recipe avoids costly offline pseudo-label preprocessing: Table 7 reports 0.2h preprocessing and 8GB storage vs. 3.4h/2.8h and 1080GB for uplifting, with <0.1s/view rasterization. Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 support its effectiveness and scaling.

Thorough ablations and analyses: teacher contribution ablation (Table 9, Table C), loss/augmentation design (Fig. 8), 3DGS-aware augmentations, robustness to 3DGS optimization and density (Table 10), iPhone RGB-D robustness (Table 11), UMAP feature visualization (Fig. G), and retrieval/scaling studies (Fig. 6, Table 8).

Reproducibility effort: codebase is released, implementation details are documented, teacher models are public, and the paper introduces/processes an InteriorGS-based 3DGS-native benchmark with per-Gaussian labels.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate relative to SceneSplat: the paper largely extends the lift-then-align paradigm from a single language teacher to multiple 2D teachers, with per-teacher projectors and losses. The core architecture and training framework are incremental rather than fundamentally new.

Several claims are stronger than the mixed evidence supports. For example, on Matterport3D zero-shot segmentation Chorus improves f-mIoU only from 10.8 to 11.4 but drops f-mAcc from 18.7 to 16.4 vs. SceneSplat. Decoder probing on ScanNet Val is worse than Sonata (75.0 vs. 77.3 mIoU), VQA METEOR is slightly lower (22.5 vs. 22.8/22.9), and instance segmentation linear probing on ScanNet Val is worse (46.9 vs. 53.9 mAP50).

Data-efficiency advantages are mainly shown against point-cloud baselines (Mosaic3D, Sonata), not against the closest 3DGS baseline SceneSplat, which uses the same 2.92K training scenes. The abstract's '8.32x' and '39.9x' comparisons therefore need careful contextualization.

Computational cost is high: Chorus has 131.3M parameters and is the slowest at 0.7s per scene (Table 12), larger/slower than SceneSplat, Sonata, and Mosaic3D. Offline teacher pseudo-label generation and online teacher inference during adaptation also remain non-trivial.

Evaluation is restricted to indoor scene understanding (semantic/instance segmentation, VQA, and point-cloud probing). The 'holistic' claim would be better supported by additional tasks such as 3D detection, captioning, navigation, or outdoor/dynamic scenes.

Some components are heuristic and only empirically justified: 3DGS-aware augmentations, visibility cropping, height-guided pose sampling, and the render-and-distill adaptation. The supplement gives plausible derivations, but the design space is large and the theoretical grounding is not exhaustive.

The point-cloud variant is trained from 3DGS-derived centers/colors/normals rather than real point clouds, so its comparison to Sonata tests cross-modal transfer under a distribution gap. This is interesting but not a clean point-cloud pretraining comparison.

The InteriorGS benchmark and label mapping are newly introduced and non-standard; while useful, the community cannot yet contextualize results against a widely established leaderboard, and it is unclear whether the processed benchmark/labels are released alongside the codebase.

strengths: Proposes a multi-teacher pretraining framework for native 3D Gaussian Splatting scene encoding, distilling language-aligned, generalist, and object-aware 2D foundation models into a shared 3D embedding with lightweight per-teacher projectors and PHI-S standardization.

Extensive empirical evaluation across semantic and instance segmentation, open-vocabulary tasks, VQA, probing/finetuning, data-efficiency settings, and domain adaptation; Chorus achieves strong gains over SceneSplat and Sonata on many benchmarks, especially on InteriorGS and several point-cloud tasks.

The render-and-distill adaptation recipe is practical: it avoids offline pseudo-label storage and enables out-of-domain finetuning with only online rendering, supported by resource and runtime analysis.

The point-cloud variant shows that the pretrained 3DGS encoder transfers effectively to point-cloud benchmarks and scales better with training scenes than self-supervised Sonata, with additional ablations and UMAP/retrieval analyses supporting the claims.
The paper is clearly written, includes detailed supplementary material on data processing, implementation, and ablations, and releases code for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The zero-shot semantic segmentation results on ScanNet200, Matterport3D, and ScanNet++ are not strictly zero-shot at the scene level, since these datasets contribute 3DGS scenes to the pretraining corpus; only InteriorGS is a genuinely unseen benchmark for new-data generalization. The paper should qualify the zero-shot claim more carefully.

The data-efficiency comparisons count only 3D training scenes and ignore the very large-scale 2D teacher pretraining (SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE-Spatial). Thus claims such as '8.32x/39.9x less training data' are better interpreted as less 3D scene data, not less total supervision or compute.

Some results are mixed rather than uniformly state-of-the-art: e.g., Chorus is lower than SceneSplat on ScanQA METEOR, lower than Mosaic3D on ScanNet200 instance mAP50, and lower than Sonata on decoder-probing ScanNetVal semantic segmentation. The broad 'state-of-the-art on a broad range of tasks' claim is somewhat overstated.

The technical novelty is primarily at the system/architecture level: multi-teacher distillation and rendering-based adaptation are adapted from existing 2D distillation and SceneSplat-style pipelines. The contribution is empirically solid but methodologically incremental.

The main paper defers important inference details for open-vocabulary segmentation to the supplement, including how language-aligned features are matched to text embeddings. Clarifying this in the main text would improve clarity and reproducibility.

The teacher ablation shows complementary gains, but there is limited analysis of redundancy or overlap among the 2D teachers beyond PHI-S standardization; a deeper analysis would strengthen the claim that the teachers provide genuinely distinct signals.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap: treating 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes as a first-class modality for general-purpose, transferable feature learning, rather than only for semantic labeling as in SceneSplat. The multi-teacher framing (language-aligned SigLIP2, generalist DINOv3, object-aware PE-Spatial) is a reasonable and principled extension of the 'lift-then-align' paradigm.

Evaluation breadth is genuinely strong: zero-shot semantic segmentation on ScanNet200/ScanNet++/Matterport3D/InteriorGS (Tab. 1), open-vocabulary instance segmentation (Tab. 2), LLM-based VQA on ScanQA/Nr3D (Tab. 3), linear/decoder probing and finetuning for semantic and instance segmentation (Tabs. 4, 6), a data-efficiency benchmark (Tab. 5), and robustness studies to 3DGS optimization/density (Tab. 10), iPhone RGB-D (Tab. 11), and model size/runtime (Tab. 12). This is a more complete empirical picture than most comparable papers.

The 3DGS-aware augmentations are a genuine, well-justified contribution. The rendering-equivalent perturbation is derived so that the first-order rendering bias vanishes and the second-order bias is controlled by η²w(α)²Σ², concentrated on low-opacity splats (Eqs. 12–16); the immature-manifold perturbation is motivated by RAIN-GS's coarse-to-fine optimization. This is a more principled design than naive point-cloud jitter and is empirically supported in Fig. 8.

The render-and-distill adaptation recipe is practically useful and well quantified: Tab. 7 shows 0.2h preprocessing vs 3.4h for uplifting and 8GB vs 1080GB storage, with the adaptation giving +2.7% mIoU on InteriorGS from only 100 scenes (Fig. 6).

Interesting and well-supported secondary finding: 3DGS pretraining acts as a strong augmentation, yielding noise-robust point-cloud features (Tab. 8, R@1 85.4% vs Sonata 79.8%; same-class@incorrect-top-1 78.0% vs 75.0%), with UMAP evidence of more compact clusters (Fig. G).

Reproducibility is above average: the supplement documents teacher pseudo-label construction, the InteriorGS 72-class mapping and LCC-based label assignment, pose sampling/visibility-crop statistics (Tab. B), and a released codebase.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty relative to the stated contribution. The core is SceneSplat plus additional 2D teachers; per-teacher projectors, shared-backbone multi-teacher distillation, and PHI-S standardization are all established in the 2D literature (DUNE, AM-RADIO, PHI-S). Crucially, there is no baseline that distills from a single fused 2D teacher (e.g., an AM-RADIO-style fused feature), which is the natural alternative and is needed to justify the multi-teacher architecture rather than simply more supervision.

The ablation support for the central claim is weak and inconsistent. Fig. 8 shows that, on ScanNet++, adding the PE-Spatial teacher from the start degrades performance (26.8 → 25.5 mIoU), that a separate staging recovers only to 26.8, and that the full multi-teacher+contrastive setup reaches just 27.1 — i.e., +0.3 mIoU over the 3DGS-augmentation-only baseline. By contrast, Tab. 9 shows a large teacher gain on ScanNet (21.2 → 29.6). The paper does not explain this discrepancy, and the ScanNet++ result undermines the framing that multi-teacher pretraining is the primary driver.

Some abstract-level claims are not supported by the evidence. Tab. 3 shows Chorus is worse than GaussianVLM on ScanQA METEOR (22.5 vs 22.9) while better on EM (14.8 vs 14.4) and R (37.4 vs 34.8), contradicting the text's 'consistent improvements on both benchmarks'. Similarly, Tab. 2 shows a head-class regression (mAP_head 18.5 vs Mosaic3D's 21.8) that is never discussed, and the VQA gains overall are small.

Headline efficiency claims are framed as marketing ratios rather than controlled evidence. '8.32× less training data' is simply 24.3/2.92 dataset ratios (Tab. 1), and the '39.9× fewer training scenes' figure is not derivable from any table in the paper. These are scene-count ratios, not matched-compute or matched-annotation comparisons.

The InteriorGS 'SoTA' claim rests on a benchmark the authors themselves constructed (processing InteriorGS [56] into a 72-class split), evaluated against a SceneSplat they retrained. Absolute numbers are low (9.0 vs 6.1 f-mIoU), so the margin is fragile and not directly comparable to prior published numbers.

The 'holistic 3DGS encoder for both 3DGS and PC inputs' claim is stretched. Point-cloud benchmarks are evaluated with a separate ● variant retrained on Gaussian centers/colors/normals, so the headline model is not itself evaluated on the point-cloud benchmarks; and the 'lightweight' framing applies only to adaptation, not pretraining, whose offline cost of running three 2D teachers over the entire pretraining set (including high-resolution DINOv3 on upsampled Matterport3D images) is never reported.

Missing comparisons to contemporaneous 3DGS-scene encoders. SceneSplat++ is cited as the 'comprehensive benchmark for language-aligned 3DGS methods' yet is not compared against, nor are other recent 3DGS encoders (e.g., GaussianSSL, LangSplat-style methods); the baseline set is essentially SceneSplat, Sonata, Mosaic3D, and PTv3.

Efficiency trade-offs are under-discussed: Tab. 12 shows Chorus is both the largest (131.3M params) and slowest (0.70s/scene) of the compared methods, which is relevant given the paper's emphasis on practicality and scalability.
